simplifications.title: One small 'house rules' plugin, not a separate guard on every card
simplifications.today: Built as written, the cards ask for about 18 in-house plugins, hook sets and wrappers; ten or more cards each bring a blocking check of their own, three plugins sit on the same outgoing text, and nine cards carry a paragraph on how they collide.
simplifications.instead: One small plugin with one blocking check and a short rule table, which is the shape your roadmap already describes. A rule is added only when a feature you picked needs it (first the reminder target, then where notes may be written), and no text is answered by a canned reply before the model sees it.
simplifications.gives_up: Each card's own separate guard, and the canned replies that skip the model (the fixed emergency line, 'last dose', a bare yes or no), so those answers depend on the cloud model being up. For the first mail step you also go without the roadmap's second, coded check on who may call the mail connector: until the plugin exists, that separation rests on tool permissions, an explicit deny on every other agent, and two tests.
simplifications.detail: The config repo holds one plugin today (home-weather). A blocking handler that throws blocks the call (plugins/hooks/reference.md:93), so every extra plugin is one more thing that can stop every tool. Roadmap lines 113, 147 and 418 ask for fail-closed hooks as one registry plugin, not one per feature. Conditions for mail before the plugin exists: the connector is allowed on the mail agent only and denied by name elsewhere; the separation check and the 'read the other parent's mail' canary are extended to it; the 'exactly one account server' test passes before go-live. The emergency reply becomes one line in the agent's instructions plus one more eval case; the existing swallowed-battery case already passes without any hook.

simplifications.title: Park the change journal, the Sunday 'what Happy did' text and 'undo that'
simplifications.today: Every tool that writes something records the change, its text and its reverse in a journal; a Sunday text reports the week to each parent; and one phrase undoes Happy's last write.
simplifications.instead: Park the card: none of the tools it would record exists yet and no other card needs it. 'What did you save about me?' is answered from that parent's own notes, and you can read the notes and OpenClaw's built-in activity record when you want to check.
simplifications.gives_up: The Sunday review text and one-phrase undo. The check on what Happy's memory kept becomes a question a parent asks, or a look by you, instead of a weekly text.
simplifications.detail: The card rates itself effort L and says most undo requests are just a second write. If you do want a weekly text, its smallest form is a no-model script that counts finished calls by tool name from OpenClaw's own audit record (on by default, 30 days, no content) and lists the note files changed that week: no journal table, no copy of note text, no undo tool. The audit query should be tried once from a scheduled command job first.

simplifications.title: No watcher scripts in the first build
simplifications.today: Five scripts poll storm alerts, team schedules, changed pages and two recall feeds, each with its own state file, plus keyword lists of what the family owns, eats and takes that nobody has written.
simplifications.instead: Write none of them now. Happy's weather answers already carry active alerts for home, each parent can switch on the phone's own severe-weather notifications, and recall emails from the agencies' own sign-ups would simply show up in the morning mail digest.
simplifications.gives_up: A text from Happy at the moment an alert is issued (Friday and Saturday evenings included), recall matching against family lists, and 'game moved' texts.
simplifications.detail: The weather plugin already fetches active alerts with every forecast (plugins/home-weather/nws.js). The card itself says no watcher gives earlier notice than the source's own service. Later, when a parent names one feed or page: subscribe a team schedule into the family calendar first (no code), and write one script for that one page only if that is not enough. The description's promise of a chore checklist was never in the build.

simplifications.title: No notification-policy plugin (daily cap, quiet hours, mute by chat)
simplifications.today: A plugin counts each parent's unprompted texts, drops any over a daily cap or outside allowed hours, and offers mute and vacation mode by chat; because a dropped text is never sent later, nine other cards carry workarounds for it.
simplifications.instead: No plugin. Each scheduled job gets a daytime hour in its schedule line, starts its text with its own label and stays silent when it has nothing to say. To quieten Happy you switch a job off, or a parent silences the thread on the phone.
simplifications.gives_up: An enforced daily cap, the urgent or not-urgent split, 'mute until 3' and a holiday pause by chat, and a backstop if a faulty job repeats itself (you would switch that job off by hand).
simplifications.detail: You have never asked for a cap or quiet hours, the card names no number and no hours, and the roadmap has no notification rule. A hook can only cancel a text, and a cancelled text is logged as a failed delivery (automation/cron-jobs/managing-jobs.md, 'A transport hook veto'). Revisit only if the family reports too many texts.

simplifications.title: No texts from one parent's Happy into the other parent's chat, and no ask-and-relay
simplifications.today: Each parent's agent is given the message tool and the 'no sends into other conversations' switch is re-opened, then an in-house check pins recipients to the family; a relay step adds a table of open requests, a yes-or-no matcher and timers. The card calls the result a small convenience and scores it 5.
simplifications.instead: Leave both switches off, as your roadmap and today's config have them: 'tell Jordan...' keeps getting a draft to send yourself. Anything meant for both parents is two scheduled jobs, one each; the one check reminders would need moves to the reminders card.
simplifications.gives_up: Happy passing a note or a yes-or-no between the two of you, and any text an agent composes to the other parent from outside its own chat.
simplifications.detail: Roadmap line 150 (no sends into other conversations; scheduled jobs deliver only to their owner) and line 493 (one data domain per person, By: You). In the live config both tools.message.crossContext switches are false. If reminders are built, the check allows add (text to the asker, no web address, an empty tool list), list and remove, and refuses update and run outright, so no job can be re-pointed at another person.

simplifications.title: Mail: one morning text with a school section, read tools only
simplifications.today: Two scheduled mail texts per parent per weekday (07:00 everything, 16:00 school), a school sender list only you can change by deploying, a check still to be built that holds the school job to those senders, a tax-season Saturday job and a second model-call tool.
simplifications.instead: One weekday 07:00 digest per connected inbox with the school lines first; the model picks out school mail from the last day's mail and relays no links. No sender list, no check, no tax-form job, no extra model tool; an afternoon school text is one more scheduled prompt if you want it.
simplifications.gives_up: A fixed sender filter (the model may miss a school mail or include one that is not), tap-through links in the school text, the weekly 'tax form still missing' line, and same-day afternoon notice unless you add the second text.
simplifications.detail: Your own reason for moving mail: 'once having the whole email inbox read, school digest would be very trivial'. Both cards say the sender filter is not a limit of the token, and the same agent already reads the whole inbox at 07:00. What limits harm is that the mail agent can only text its owner (roadmap line 402). Health mail: sender and subject only, as one prompt line. If a parent ever agrees to school mail and nothing else, a check on the search would be that parent's one limit in code and comes back as an open item. Look at the first two weeks of real digests before touching any school platform's settings.

simplifications.title: Photos and PDFs: one switch and one test, no privacy-gate plugin
simplifications.today: Before photos and PDFs are switched on, an in-house plugin is built to refuse a PDF whose text looks like a bank statement or tax form; it cannot check photos or scans, and whether it can see PDF text at all is untested.
simplifications.instead: Switch attachment reading on with one setting once you have answered the data-retention question, keep audio understanding off, and add one test: a PDF with hidden instructions must cause no tool call, a hand-off to the web helper included. One line on the printed sheet: no bank, tax or medical papers.
simplifications.gives_up: A tripwire that would refuse a text PDF that looks like a statement, sent by mistake. Photos and scans of the same page were never covered.
simplifications.detail: The gate appears in the records only as the assistant's proposed condition inside a question; the card calls it 'the condition Tony set'. The roadmap asks for no screening of a parent's own attachments, and the wave B mail decision sends the same kinds of document unscreened. Settings: channels.imessage.includeAttachments true, tools.media.audio.enabled false. The caveat about a later on-device classifier is deleted.

simplifications.title: Two places for family facts, not four
simplifications.today: The first wave sets up four homes for what the family knows: each parent's notes, facts rendered into every chat, a shared handbook with a wiki plugin, and a shared database with its own tools.
simplifications.instead: Start with two: facts you type into the family file, rendered into the files the generator already writes, and each parent's own saved notes. A plain shared handbook folder joins only after its untested search passes; the database and the wiki step wait for a picked feature that needs them.
simplifications.gives_up: A parent changing a shared fact by text (they tell you, or keep it on a shared list on the phone), saving a handbook page by texting a photo, and Happy answering 'when is the filter due?' from its own data.
simplifications.detail: No wave A card needs the database; its users are later cards, most of which other entries here park or shrink. Render facts into USER.md (4,000-character cap) or a section of AGENTS.md and leave MEMORY.md to OpenClaw: the generator renders four files today and the deploy script deliberately never touches MEMORY.md or the memory folder. 'Filter every 90 days' is a repeating calendar event or reminder. If the database is built later: typed, short inputs instead of a separate secret detector, and no fact_get or fact_set tools in its first version.

simplifications.title: Scheduled jobs: three switches and one short script, not a generator with a charter per job
simplifications.today: A generator creates, compares and removes every scheduled job from the family file and writes a charter per job into the agent's instructions, placed in the first wave, where at most one job would use it, and scored 5.
simplifications.instead: Now: three scheduler safety switches, with failure alerts routed to you. Jobs: one short checked-in script that creates each job with the owner's handle read from the family file, a time limit and a tool list on every job, and the job's rules in its own message.
simplifications.gives_up: Per-person on and off switches in the family file, the written charter, and automatic clean-up of jobs that no longer match the file; a changed job is edited by hand until an edit step is written.
simplifications.detail: The card itself says the three switches are plain config and that a charter is prompt text, not enforcement. Switches: cron.failureAlert to the operator, cron.skipMissedJobs true, cron.triggers.enabled false. Roadmap line 142 wants delivery targets generated from the family file and never typed by hand, so the script reads them from it. Jobs keep the normal context, so the Hard rules section still loads on every run. The generator should never talk to the Gateway itself: it writes a jobs file and the deploy script applies it. Build the comparing generator when the script holds more jobs than can be read at a glance.

simplifications.title: One evening brief for you, not three briefs for each parent
simplifications.today: Six scheduled texts for two people (evening, Sunday week-ahead, weekday morning), a rule that both parents tag every calendar event with who drives, a gear table, and extra reads from the database and from a second mail job.
simplifications.instead: One evening text for you: tomorrow's calendar, the forecast and any active alert, silent when nothing is on, at a time you set; its Sunday run covers the week ahead. It waits for the calendar answer.
simplifications.gives_up: A separate morning brief and Sunday text, the 'who drives' and 'what to pack' lines, and email deadlines repeated in the brief unless someone put them on the calendar.
simplifications.detail: The roadmap plans one scheduled text only, the 07:00 mail digest. The driver tag and the gear table were made up by an agent, and by the card's own caveat they are most of what the brief adds over the daily digest Google's Gemini app can already send. A hand-off of mail dates from the mail agent into the parent's agent would cut against roadmap line 402 (a mail agent's only output is its scheduled text). The card still calls the mail card 'wave C'.

simplifications.title: Dates become reminders, or calendar events you add; no calendar-write server and no renewals table
simplifications.today: To put dates on the family calendar the card needs an in-house write server around the connector, its own write token, an approval check and a two-step confirmation never tried on iMessage; renewals get a generated table, a monthly script with lead-time rules and a job per parent.
simplifications.instead: After reading a flyer Happy lists the dates in full and, after your yes, sets reminders once reminders exist; you add calendar events on the phone. Each expiry or upkeep date is one calendar event with an alert, typed once, which also works when Happy is down.
simplifications.gives_up: Happy putting a season schedule on the shared calendar (until a parent adds the events, they are not in calendar answers or the evening brief), one combined monthly 'coming due' text, and upkeep intervals that restart by chat.
simplifications.detail: The card's own caveat calls the calendar write the optional, later step that 'need not be built'. The connector has no calendar write tool, so the wrapper is new code, and roadmap line 418 requires an approval enforced in code if a write is ever built, so the only simpler design is not building it yet. A five-minute hand test (send one calendar file from Messages on the Mac, tap it on each phone) settles whether a tap-to-add file could ever replace the write route. Nobody has said which passports, cars or domains exist.

simplifications.title: A routine is a few reviewed lines in Happy's instructions; no skills pipeline yet
simplifications.today: To teach Happy a routine the card adds a file-reading permission on the agents that hold private notes, a deploy step for skill folders and a write-protection proof, with a ten-question practice quiz fixed as the first skill.
simplifications.instead: Until there are more routines than fit comfortably, a routine is a reviewed section of the agent's instruction file, deployed as today, with nothing new granted. Nothing is built until one of you names a first routine.
simplifications.gives_up: Routines loaded only when needed, a '/skill' shortcut, and the practice quiz as a named first deliverable, with its re-quiz reminder and read-aloud extras.
simplifications.detail: Skills inside each agent stay the roadmap's long-term home for know-how (line 492, By: You); this is a deferral, not a reversal, and it is the tighter option because it adds no file-read grant. The card itself says a routine of a few lines can live in AGENTS.md, and no parent has described one yet.

simplifications.title: Waves C, D and Later become one 'parked' list with a one-line note each
simplifications.today: Twelve items, four rated value 2 and five rated large, each keep a full build design and between them four open decisions, all of which have to be kept true while OpenClaw changes weekly.
simplifications.instead: Keep A and B, the letters you steer by, as the list you pick from. Fold the rest into one parked list, one line per item and no open decision; four are labelled as roadmap milestones not yet scheduled (trips, email to the asker, the research browser, kids).
simplifications.gives_up: A pre-set order among the parked items and their ready-made designs on the page. The designs stay in the data files and would be redone around whatever you eventually ask for.
simplifications.detail: Extras cut from parked cards whatever you decide later: the Home Assistant, TV and spoken-announcement branch on F076; realtime cloud voice and the second-phone branch on OCL-01; the full virtual-machine design on MAC-02 (kept as a parked note with one 'step zero' test and no fallback to a real desktop); the billed Google place lookup, the Friday text and the passport line on F028; the Sunday dinner job, recipe box and schema step on F033; the tax-receipts list on CRT-11; the self-pacing job on AUT-01 (a note plus one ordinary recurring reminder does it); link download on F080 (attached files only); the daily send cap on F049; one agent per child on F072 (the roadmap has one shared kids agent). F020 is built only if a month of web reading shows unreadable pages someone cared about.

simplifications.title: Three operator cards shrink to one check and a few lines on paper
simplifications.today: A script texts both parents when the model is down and again when it is back; a 20-entry device deny list is deployed for devices that are not paired; a daily health job, a scheduled audit with change comparison and checklist texts all run through Happy.
simplifications.instead: No outage script: one line on the printed sheet says what Happy's error text means. The deny list becomes step one of whichever card first pairs a device. One daily check is added with mail (is the Google sign-in still valid), reporting the way your existing checks do; audits and drills stay commands you run on the roadmap's schedule.
simplifications.gives_up: An unprompted 'model is down' text to both parents, a written limit in config before any device exists (a device paired by mistake before then is not covered), automatic comparison of audit results, and check results arriving in the iMessage thread.
simplifications.detail: You already get model and gateway alerts by ntfy (roadmap line 447) and a parent who texts during an outage already sees an error line. The roadmap still requires the audit monthly and after every update and the quarterly restore drill (lines 433 and 510): they become calendar reminders for you, not a scheduled job. The one documented deny line for screen control (computer.act) can ride along in any deploy if you want a visible 'no' today. Also dropped: fixed reminders rebuilt as no-model jobs, eval fixtures for tools that do not exist yet, the standing check for a plugin that does nothing without the Mac app, and the Legacy Contact line on the recovery card.

simplifications.title: Small extras come off cards that stay
simplifications.today: Several kept cards carry extras nobody asked for: a scripted 'on it' and 'cancel that' for web lookups, a fixed fact-check verdict with a 30-day staleness rule, three routes to a nicer voice, a snowfall number from a third weather feed, a per-job ownership lookup for reminders.
simplifications.instead: Web reading keeps one time limit and one rule: give the link and the time fetched, show the page's own date, say 'could not verify'. Spoken replies, if ever built, use the built-in Mac voice. The weather upgrade is the hourly forecast only.
simplifications.gives_up: 'Cancel that' in plain words for a running lookup, a uniform true, false, mixed or unclear verdict shape, a snowfall amount in numbers on day one, editing a reminder in place, and written-down options for a nicer voice.
simplifications.detail: The card records the 30-day figure and the link cap as house choices with no source and says nothing enforces them; the cancel phrase would mean one more tool on the parents' agents. The snowfall field exists but comes in millimetres over mostly six-hour intervals, so it would not give an hour-by-hour amount. Add any of these back when a real answer shows the need.

questions.question: You put mail in wave B. Do you want it built first, ahead of the rest of wave A, as a short ordered list: mail for your inbox, then web reading, then photos and PDFs? And which five items in the catalog are your own top picks?
questions.why: It sets the order of everything: today 19 wave A items, six of them plumbing a parent would not notice, sit in front of the mail you have asked about three times, and the value scores that rank them are the assistant's.
questions.default: Yes: mail first, then one item at a time, each live only after its own test. The rest of wave A becomes an unordered 'next' list you pick from, ordered by your marks and not by the score. If you say no, mail stays behind wave A as it is today.

questions.question: About the children and school, to answer once: (1) how many children are there and which school year is each in, and may that be written in the family file? (2) Does any child have their own Apple device? (3) Which school systems send you email, and does the school already text or push urgent notices itself? (4) Any team or activity app? (5) Camps, a sitter or grandparents who help? (6) Does either of you write or speak to Happy in a language other than English?
questions.why: About fifteen cards are written around two children aged 8 and 10, a soccer team, a sitter, grandparents and replies in Chinese; the family file records two adults and nothing else.
questions.default: A card whose premise you do not confirm is parked. Examples say 'the kids' with no number, age or name. English only. The school is assumed to send its own urgent alerts. Nothing new is rendered into every chat until you type the facts yourself.

questions.question: Which of these, which nobody on record has asked for, do you actually want? Voice memos and spoken replies (F003); a three-way group chat with Happy (F006); long answers emailed to you (F049); summaries of a video or podcast from a link (F020); lights and speakers by text (F076); printing (F080: is the Canon photo printer the one you would use?); the OpenClaw app on your iPhone (OCL-01); project check-ins every few days (AUT-01); a weekly dinner-plan text (F033); a childcare coverage planner (CRT-11); a calendar conflict watch (MKT-06); a dose log when a child is ill (CRT-10); a sitter sheet or school-form kit (CRT-13); a weekly 'what Happy did' text (G006).
questions.why: Each came from a network scan, a vendor page or a general source, not from you or Jordan, and most have a full design waiting on a yes.
questions.default: None is built; each keeps one line on the parked list. Groups stay disabled, as M1 signed off. The one-page emergency plan stays available as an ordinary chat request. Asked about a dose, Happy suggests a shared note kept with the medicine and never advises a dose.

questions.question: Where do you and Jordan keep family events today: one shared Google calendar, one shared iCloud calendar, each on your own, or nowhere? Are the kids' activities and school dates on it, and do you mark who drives? And do you share any Apple Reminders list (groceries, errands) you would want Happy to add to?
questions.why: Twelve cards read 'the family Google Calendar' or 'the shared grocery list' as facts; neither has ever been stated, and on iCloud there is no proven route.
questions.default: The calendar card stays written for Google but nothing is built on it: calendar answers, the evening brief and the conflict watch wait. No driver or packing line. The Reminders bridge leaves wave A until there is a list you both use and the by-hand test passes.

questions.question: Is there an hour before or after which you do not want a scheduled text from Happy, and may anything (a storm alert, say) text you at night? For mail: one text a day with the school lines first, or two (everything at 07:00 and a school text in the afternoon), and at what time?
questions.why: 07:00 for the mail digest is the only time in your roadmap; 16:00, 18:00, 19:30 and 22:30 were all picked by agents.
questions.default: No window is set or enforced. One mail text on weekdays at 07:00, about ten lines, school lines first, no afternoon text. Every other job gets a daytime hour you set when you switch it on, and any job that would text at night needs its own yes.

questions.question: Do you want timed reminder texts from Happy ('remind me at 4:30') built now? They would work for you only, and the phone already sets a timed reminder by voice.
questions.why: It means giving the scheduling tool to the agent that holds your notes, which OpenClaw advises against for agents that read outside content, plus a check to make that safe; ten cards offer reminders through it.
questions.default: Not in the first steps: the scheduling tool stays off every agent and Happy keeps today's answer (it cannot set reminders; use the phone). It is the likely second step. If you say yes: your agent only, after one live test that a reminder can be created from iMessage at all.

questions.question: Which scheduled texts does Jordan want, and has she agreed to connect her own Gmail?
questions.why: Digests, briefs, watchers and reviews are all specified as one job per parent, but nothing records what she wants, and only she can approve her inbox on Google's screen.
questions.default: Each feature is set up and tuned for you first, the order M1 used. Her copy of any text is switched on when she asks, and her Gmail and calendar sign-ins only when she approves them herself. Until then the school lines from your inbox cover the school mail, since you both receive it.

questions.question: Until OpenAI answers on Zero Data Retention, may these go to the cloud model, where abuse-monitoring logs can keep them for up to 30 days: (1) the text of your own mail; (2) photos and PDFs you choose to send; (3) your children's health details (doses, allergies, conditions) that Happy would store and re-send?
questions.why: The summary marks mail as decided with no options and recommends switching photos on now, but you are on record only as agreeing to apply, and your roadmap says retention is to be handled before a private agent uses OpenAI. The first step waits on this answer.
questions.default: Wait. Everything is set up and tested, but real mail is read only once OpenAI approves or you say 'go ahead'; photos and PDFs stay off, as they are today; children's health details are not stored. The assistant's own recommendation is to go ahead for your inbox and for photos you choose to send, with one house rule (no bank, tax or medical papers): your chats with Happy already go to the same model on the same terms.

questions.question: When you said 'no need' to add Jordan to the command list, did you also mean (a) she needs no way of her own to stop Happy by text, and (b) she is not made a command owner, so timed reminders and project check-ins are yours only?
questions.why: The summary read your answer as 'she needs another way' and filed a stop plugin with four hooks, a kill file and a lock-out phrase under 'decided'; three cards still list making her an owner as an open decision.
questions.default: Yes to both. The stop card becomes one printed sheet of the built-in commands for you; stopping everything stays the scheduler switch and stopping the gateway at the Mac; Jordan's stop is to tell you, or to shut the Mac mini down. No lock-out phrase: a lost phone is handled with Lost Mode and by you removing the handle. This gives up one text from either parent that halts everything. When Jordan sends a flyer, Happy lists the dates and she adds them herself.

questions.question: Your rule is one data domain per person. Do you want a shared household place that both your agent and Jordan's read (a handbook folder now, a small database later), and may anything personal sit in it? Should Happy also keep an excerpt of each chat when it resets overnight? And would you write and keep up a few pages of household facts?
questions.why: Two cards call their store 'shared by design', and one planned table would hold copies of each parent's private notes, without a shared place ever being put to you.
questions.default: Yes, for household facts only (dates, appliance details, provider contacts); each parent's own notes, and any copy of them, stay out. No chat excerpts: Happy keeps only what a parent asks it to remember, as today. One handbook page that you add to when the same question comes up twice.

questions.question: Do the roadmap's safety gates still apply to the first steps? Before mail: a firewall rule that lets the mail connector talk to Google only, and one planted-mail test. Before web reading: the home-network and hand-off tests, and the outbound proxy, which you can build first as the roadmap says or waive in writing for the plain page-fetch tool.
questions.why: The roadmap calls its security track not optional, you skipped local models but not that track, and no card builds or counts these controls.
questions.default: Yes, in their cheapest form, shown as a prerequisite on each card. With no answer on the proxy the roadmap stands: web reading waits for it.

questions.question: How often are you away overnight while Jordan is at home, and is she willing to type one password at the Mac after a power cut? Should she also get the 'Happy is down' alert? And should failed-job alerts reach you as an iMessage from Happy, or on ntfy like your other alerts?
questions.why: The recovery card assumes both, while the roadmap row you chose says Happy stays down after a power cut until you unlock it.
questions.default: Print only the half page that tells her how to recognise that Happy is down and that nothing is broken: no envelope, no Terminal steps, no alert to her. Failed-job alerts come by iMessage, noted on the card as a deliberate exception so that raw error text is not sent to an outside push service.

questions.question: What may Happy put into a public web search or hand to the web helper: the home town, a child's age, a child's name, the school's name?
questions.why: The card settles this itself ('ages yes, names and school no') as a prompt rule you never stated, and one example writes an age in.
questions.default: Town and ages yes, names and school no, marked on the card as 'default, not yet confirmed'.

questions.question: Is 'nothing a child types goes to a cloud model' your own rule, whatever a vendor's terms say? And when the kids agent is built, is the roadmap's weekly list of flagged exchanges enough oversight?
questions.why: The kids card is parked on that rule, which appears only in roadmap text an agent wrote, with a '13+' reason that could not be confirmed; the card also widened oversight to a nightly digest of everything each child asked.
questions.default: Yes: it is recorded as a house rule confirmed by you, and the kids agent stays parked until a local model exists. Oversight is the weekly flagged list; chat hours are set in Screen Time on the child's device; the nightly digest and an instant alert are listed as options.

questions.question: Should 'OpenClaw documents it' count as a reason an item is worth having, or only as proof that it can be built?
questions.why: 23 of the 42 'Backed by' lines point at OpenClaw's own bundled docs or skills, and that test removed none of 162 items.
questions.default: Proof only: the line is renamed 'Can be built because', and worth rests on what you say you want.

tests_first.what: That a read-only Gmail token from a home-made, published Google sign-in app keeps working past seven days on a personal account. Every mail feature rests on it; the card lists it as untested while its prerequisites state it as settled.
tests_first.test: Set up the Google project, publish the sign-in app, sign in your own account with the read-only Gmail grant, and run one mail search on day 1 and again on day 8 or later. If the day-8 search fails, the choice is a weekly sign-in per parent or a different connector, and you make it before the rest of the mail step is built.

tests_first.what: That each agent can reach only its own account connector, and that a calendar sign-in for the same Google account cannot read mail. The roadmap lists the first as not yet confirmed on this version.
tests_first.test: Once the connector is installed: list each agent's tools and confirm the mail agent shows only its own Gmail read tools and no other agent shows them; ask an eval-only clone of another agent to read your mail and confirm it is refused. Before calendar questions go live, add the calendar-only sign-in, stored apart from the mail one, and confirm it cannot run a mail search.

tests_first.what: That the deploy path can reach Happy's scheduler at all, and whether adding the same job twice under a fixed key updates it instead of duplicating it.
tests_first.test: Add one read-only 'list all jobs' line to the inspect script and run it once. Then add one throwaway job twice under the same fixed key, the second time with a changed message, and list again. One job carrying the new message means the jobs file needs no comparison step; two jobs means keeping a name-keyed comparison. If the list call fails, the jobs design is not buildable as written.

tests_first.what: That a web lookup handed to the research helper returns its answer to the parent's agent while agents stay unable to see each other's sessions. The roadmap lists this as not yet confirmed, yet the card is marked ready now.

notes: Nothing was changed by this review. No OpenClaw command was run and no device was contacted; the reviewers read the cards, the installed docs and code, and the config repo, and almost nothing here was tried live. That is why there is a 'tests first' list.

This list is built from 208 findings that survived a second reviewer's challenge; 13 were overturned and are left out. In this last step I re-read the roadmap, the fact sheet, the summary and all 221 finding rows, and spot-checked the live config (groups disabled, attachments off, cross-conversation sends off, one plugin in the repo), the deploy and generator scripts, a handful of installed doc lines cited here, and seven cards (the six in the first slice and the jobs card). I did not re-open the other 35 cards or any web page.
'Saves' (S, M, L) and the card counts beside each question are estimates, with no unit in hours, the same weakness this review found in the catalog's own effort chips.

Hard-rule check, data retention: the reviewers disagreed on the default. One proposed 'yes, start on your own inbox'; two proposed waiting. I took 'wait', because your roadmap says OpenAI's 30-day retention is to be handled before a private agent uses OpenAI and nothing you have said waives that. The 'go ahead' recommendation is shown beside it.

Hard-rule check, the house-rules plugin: building it second, after mail, leaves the first mail step without the roadmap's coded check on who may call an account connector. Tool permissions and an explicit deny are still limits the model cannot talk its way past, but it is one layer, not two. If you want two, the plugin and the hook test come before mail.

Hard-rule check, the first step: reading mail on the cloud model departs from the roadmap's 'mail on a local model only' rule. That follows from your own choices (local models skipped, mail in wave B); the roadmap's mail exit test 'the reader makes no network calls' cannot hold as written and is replaced by the firewall rule and the planted-mail test. The lookup that brings mail text into your main agent is kept out of the first step.

Repaired to keep roadmap rules: the jobs script reads each owner's handle from the family file, never typed in (line 142); the reminders check refuses update and run so no job can be re-pointed at another person (line 150); the research browser's guard, if ever built, is an allowlist of read-only actions, because clicking and typing could fill a booking form or tick a CAPTCHA box, both on your never list; the monthly audit, the audit after every update and the quarterly restore drill stay, as your own cadence; routines in the instruction file are a deferral of 'skills inside each agent', not a reversal.

Left out of the simplifications on purpose: giving house-device tools straight to each parent's agent (it depends on how you read your own 'one agent per permission set' rule, and the card is parked anyway), and replacing the roadmap's mail-out server and recipient check with a send tool that has no recipient field (it meets the 'only to the asker' rule more strictly but departs from the mechanism the roadmap names). Both come back as questions if those cards are picked.
With no answer on the outbound proxy, the default keeps the roadmap's gate, so web reading (step 2) waits for the proxy or for your written waiver.

Where reviewers disagreed on a design I took the plan-level verdict and put the other in 'detail': the change journal (park, versus a smallest weekly text), renewals (calendar events, versus one table in the database), the school digest (no sender list, versus a sender list without a check).

Questions and tests that matter only if a parked card is picked are held back: the sender account for emailed answers, whose sign-in reads calendars for the conflict watch, whether a Google Cloud account with a card on file is acceptable for place lookup, one volume cap for the speakers, the group-chat history test, the thirty-second print test from a phone, and two checks on the Control UI already on your phone.
One claim rests on a web search summary only: that the printer the scan saw is a large-format photo printer. The maker's page refused a direct fetch.
Items removed in earlier rounds were not brought back, and no value score or wave was changed.
